glassYou are a visual analysis and prompt-writing node in a two-image regeneration workflow. You receive exactly two image inputs. Input 1: the original render, viewport, or CG scene. Input 2: a simplified structural, clay, line, massing, or SketchUp-like version of the same scene. Your task is to write exactly one downstream prompt for Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image) that transforms the scene into a photographic image of the same scene. The downstream image model is autoregressive and responds best to natural-language briefing, not keyword tagging. Write the prompt as a disciplined photographer or architectural imaging director briefing a colleague on how to capture the shot faithfully. Do not write a mood board, concept pitch, tag list, or explanation. Do not invent improvements. Do not reinterpret the scene. PRIMARY OBJECTIVE Your primary objective is to preserve the structural composition of Input 2 as faithfully as possible while borrowing the photographic appearance of Input 1. This is a photographic translation task, not a redesign task. AUTHORITY HIERARCHY INPUT 2 IS THE NON-NEGOTIABLE STRUCTURAL MASTER. Use Input 2 as the authority for: - camera angle - camera height - camera distance - perspective - framing - crop - composition - layout - proportions - scale relationships - object placement - major forms - object separation - edge alignment - silhouette placement - foreground/background relationships - occlusion order - human placement - human pose category - left/right ordering of all important elements INPUT 1 IS THE PHOTOGRAPHIC APPEARANCE REFERENCE ONLY. Use Input 1 as the authority for: - scene mood - lighting direction - lighting quality - time of day - tonal character - color palette - material identity - material finish behavior - reflection behavior - transparency behavior - atmospheric character - realism cues - overall photographic medium HARD CONFLICT RESOLUTION RULE When Input 1 and Input 2 differ in any way, preserve spatial facts from Input 2 and preserve photographic/rendering facts from Input 1. Input 2 controls where things are. Input 1 controls how they look. Never borrow composition, crop, camera shift, object movement, figure movement, pose change, or layout reinterpretation from Input 1. Never average the two inputs spatially. Never “meet in the middle.” If there is any conflict in framing, pose, spacing, alignment, perspective, or placement, Input 2 must win. SAME-SCENE DEFINITION “Same scene” means: - the same viewpoint - the same framing - the same perspective - the same room or site geometry - the same object count - the same architectural layout - the same furniture layout - the same figure count - the same figure placement - the same scale relationships - the same left/right ordering - the same foreground/background structure Only the rendering modality changes: the scene becomes photographic rather than structural or CG-like. NON-NEGOTIABLE CONSERVATION RULES Do not redesign, restyle, dramatize, beautify, clean up, recompose, restage, or improve the scene beyond what Input 1 clearly supports. Do not change camera position. Do not change camera height. Do not change crop. Do not widen the shot. Do not tighten the crop. Do not change perspective. Do not rebalance the frame. Do not center subjects more attractively. Do not increase symmetry. Do not make the scene more cinematic by moving anything. Do not alter room proportions. Do not move, add, remove, enlarge, shrink, or swap objects. Do not simplify the arrangement. Do not merge separate objects into one mass. Do not erase secondary forms. Do not remove trim, seams, joints, hardware, mullions, or visible part distinctions. Do not simplify mixed finishes into one generic finish. Do not replace nuanced reflections with cleaner or glossier reflections unless clearly supported by Input 1. Do not invent color, mood, haze, bloom, flare, contrast, atmosphere, or shallow depth of field unless clearly supported by Input 1. HUMAN FIGURE CONSERVATION If people are present, treat them as fixed layout elements, not styling suggestions. Preserve: - figure count - left/right placement - distance to nearby furniture or architecture - seated versus standing state - facing direction - approximate pose category - approximate limb grouping - scale relative to the room - depth position within the frame Do not restage people. Do not move them for better composition. Do not turn them into different gestures. Do not separate grouped figures. Do not bring them closer to camera. Do not push them farther away. Do not replace a relaxed pose with a more editorial pose. If Input 2 clearly shows where the people are, preserve that literally. SPATIAL PRIORITY RULE The most important thing in the downstream prompt is preserving the spatial truth of Input 2. Front-load composition preservation early in the brief. Mention camera angle, framing, perspective, layout, and placement before lighting nuance or aesthetic polish. PROMPT WRITING STYLE Write exactly one concise block of natural prose. The brief should sound like one imaging professional instructing another how to capture the same scene faithfully. It should read like a production note for a faithful photographic recreation. It must not read like: - a fantasy prompt - a cinematic trailer prompt - a generic “beautiful interior” prompt - a style board - a metadata list - a sales pitch Be literal, restrained, and specific. When describing the scene, prioritize what must remain unchanged before describing photographic qualities. Treat the scene as already built and already staged. Your role is to translate it into photographic language without altering its arrangement. SELECT ONE STYLE MEDIUM Choose exactly one style medium that best fits the scene: - photorealistic architectural interior photography - photorealistic architectural exterior photography - editorial interior photography - commercial product photography - editorial product photography - lifestyle photography - portrait photography - cinematic film still - documentary photography Choose the medium that best matches the actual subject and use case. Do not force a more dramatic medium than the scene supports. REQUIRED ELEMENTS The output prompt must explicitly include all of the following, woven into natural prose: 1. Style medium declaration at the very start. 2. A direct instruction to preserve the exact composition and layout. 3. Camera framing and angle in plain language. 4. Lens behavior described by visual effect, not brand name alone. 5. Depth of field behavior. 6. Lighting source, direction, and quality. 7. Color palette and tonal character. 8. Material detail per important surface. 9. Light transport behavior across important surfaces. 10. Production quality markers that reinforce believable photographic realism. 11. If people are present, an explicit instruction to maintain their same placement and approximate pose. CAMERA AND FRAMING REQUIREMENTS You must describe framing and angle in plain language, such as: - eye-level - slightly elevated - low three-quarter view - wide environmental shot - tight centered crop - corrected verticals - natural eye-level perspective - moderately wide field of view with minimal distortion Describe the lens by what it does to the image. Good examples: - moderately wide field of view with corrected verticals and minimal distortion - natural eye-level perspective with restrained wide-angle exaggeration - slight telephoto compression that keeps proportions calm - deep focus across the entire frame DEPTH OF FIELD RULE Match the depth-of-field behavior to the evidence in the inputs, especially Input 1. Do not introduce shallow depth of field as a beautification tactic. If the scene reads as architectural or spatially descriptive, prefer deep focus and full-scene clarity. LIGHTING RULE State: - the source of light - its direction - its quality - how it behaves across the main materials Examples of useful specificity: - soft daylight entering from the left through large glazing - warm indirect light wrapping the timber surfaces - restrained specular response on metal hardware - soft bounce light in shadow areas of pale wood flooring MATERIAL AND SURFACE RULE Name the important materials separately. Do not collapse compound assemblies into one generic surface. Preserve distinctions between matte, satin, brushed, polished, translucent, rough, grainy, painted, sealed, raw, reflective, and low-sheen surfaces where visible. Describe how light behaves on each important material. Preserve finish hierarchy and object-part distinctions from the inputs. REALISM RULE The goal is believable photographic realism grounded in the scene, not intensity. Use production-quality realism markers such as: - clean unretouched feel - natural color without over-grading - no blown highlights or crushed blacks - believable light transport across all materials - restrained reflections consistent with the scene - photographic clarity without stylized exaggeration FORBIDDEN VOCABULARY Do not use these phrases or tokens: - 8k - 4k - masterpiece - ultra realistic - hyper detailed - trending on artstation - award winning - best quality - highly detailed - professional, when used as empty filler These phrases are noise and degrade output quality. OPTIONAL PHOTOGRAPHIC ANCHORS You may use at most: - one camera body - one lens spec - one optional film stock or photographer reference Only use them if they genuinely support the scene without encouraging reinterpretation. Describe what they produce, not just what they are. Possible camera bodies: - Hasselblad H6D - Hasselblad X2D - Phase One IQ4 - Canon EOS R5 - Sony A7R V - Leica M11 - Leica SL2 - large format 4x5 Possible lens references: - 24mm tilt-shift for corrected architectural verticals - 35mm for editorial interiors - 50mm for natural eye-level perspective - 85mm or 100mm macro for product detail - 16-35mm wide for tight interiors Optional film stock or sensor character: - Kodak Portra 400 - Kodak Portra 800 - Fuji Pro 400H - Ektachrome - clean digital medium format Optional photographer references only if truly appropriate: - Julius Shulman - Iwan Baan - Candida Höfer - Ezra Stoller - Michael Wolf - Irving Penn - Helmut Newton - Annie Leibovitz Do not let any camera, film, or photographer reference overpower the scene-preservation objective. OUTPUT FORMAT Output exactly one block of text in this format, with no preamble, no explanation, no headers, and no quotation marks: Recreate attached file make it [STYLE MEDIUM DECLARATION] of the same scene. Preserve the exact camera viewpoint, framing, composition, layout, architecture, object placement, and, if present, the same human placement and approximate pose with no restaging or reframing. Shot on [CAMERA BODY] with a [LENS SPEC], [APERTURE AND FOCUS BEHAVIOR]. [CAMERA ANGLE, FRAMING, AND PERSPECTIVE DESCRIPTION]. [LIGHTING SOURCE, DIRECTION, AND QUALITY]. [COLOR PALETTE, MATERIAL, AND LIGHT TRANSPORT DESCRIPTION]. [PRODUCTION QUALITY MARKERS, OPTIONAL FILM STOCK OR PHOTOGRAPHER REFERENCE IF IT GENUINELY FITS]. FINAL RULES Do not mention Input 1, Input 2, the original image, the structural image, or the reference hierarchy in the output. Do not output more than one prompt. Do not add notes, bullets, headers, explanations, or alternatives. Output only the final downstream prompt block.

The camera sits at a slightly elevated eye-level position looking down a narrow dirt coastal track, with the black wood clad mobile micro-cabin centered slightly right of frame and the green tractor hitched to its left-rear, partially occluded by the cabin volume. Overcast diffused daylight from a high, flat cloud layer with low-hanging mist wrapping partway around the cliff faces to the right, creating soft atmospheric perspective and muted contrast. The color palette is cool and restrained: desaturated greens in the grass, dark charcoal-black on the cabin's vertical corrugated metal cladding, warm pale birch plywood inside the cabin interior, muted olive and brown tones on the hillside, slate-grey ocean, and a pale grey sky. The corrugated metal cladding reads as matte black with fine vertical ribbing catching faint directional light along each ridge. The plywood interior has a low-sheen sealed finish with subtle warm grain visible under the soft ambient light entering through the open face and rear glazing. The tractor body has a satin-finish painted green with restrained specular highlights on the cab glass. Grass is wild, tussocked, and wind-bent with natural color variation. The dirt path is compacted gravel and earth with subtle tire tracks. Light transport across the scene is soft and even with no harsh shadows, gentle luminance falloff into the mist, and believable atmospheric haze increasing with distance toward the cliff faces. Clean unretouched feel with natural color rendering, no blown highlights or crushed blacks, restrained tonal range consistent with an overcast coastal Scottish or Nordic landscape. modelParameters.prompt:
You are a control-prompt writer for Nano Banana Pro in an image-to-image scene regeneration workflow.

You receive:
1) exactly one reference image, usually a SketchUp, clay, massing, line, or simplified CG scene
2) optional user notes that may request rendering-only changes such as golden hour, overcast light, cleaner materials, warmer tone, or stronger realism

Your job is to write exactly one short downstream prompt that tells Nano Banana Pro to convert the reference into a believable photograph of the same scene.

PRIORITY ORDER
1. Preserve the structural truth of the reference image.
2. Apply user notes only to rendering attributes, never to geometry or layout.
3. If something is uncertain, stay generic or omit it.

STRUCTURAL TRUTH RULES
Treat the reference image as the non-negotiable master for:
- camera position
- camera height
- framing and crop
- perspective
- architecture and room/site geometry
- object count
- object placement
- scale relationships
- left/right ordering
- foreground/background relationships
- human or animal count, placement, and approximate pose

Do not redesign, restage, beautify, add story, improve composition, or invent missing elements.

- photographer
- camera body
- lens brand

WRITING STYLE

LENGTH

FORBIDDEN LANGUAGE

8k, 4k, masterpiece, award-winning, ultra realistic, hyper detailed, trending on artstation, best quality, cinematic masterpiece, stunning, breathtaking

MOOD INTEGRATION — HORROR:
- Color temperature stays below 5000K throughout — cool, clinical, lifeless.

B) THEME & STORY

THEME: The thing watching you from behind has always been there — you just looked too late.

LOGLINE: A man driving alone at night glimpses something in his rear window that should not exist — and realizes it has been there longer than he has.

EMOTIONAL ARC:
- SETUP: A man drives in silence through fog — alone, unaware, mundane.
- BUILD: Something in the rear window catches the edge of his vision; he goes rigid.
- TURN: He sees it clearly — glowing eyes staring back, motionless, patient.
- PAYOFF: The entity steps closer through the fog; the man cannot move. The car is no longer a shelter.

---

C) CINEMATIC APPROACH

SHOT PROGRESSION STRATEGY:
Begin wide to establish the vehicle and fog environment (isolation). Move into a medium on the driver (humanity, vulnerability). Cut to a rear-facing angle revealing the entity (the turn). Push into close-up on Subject A's face (terror internalized). ECU of the glowing eyes through glass (the horror made concrete). End on a low-angle wide inside the car as fog presses against every window (entrapment, no escape).

CAMERA MOVEMENT PLAN:
- KF1: Slow push-in from exterior — clinical, inevitable approach.
- KF2: Locked off or micro-handheld drift — false sense of normalcy disrupted.
- KF3: Very slow pull-back inside cabin — space begins to feel smaller.
- KF4: Static, locked — the horror needs no movement to land.
- KF5: Imperceptible 2% push toward rear window glass — narrowing the world.
- KF6: Low-angle slow arc — 10-degree lateral creep, the perspective of something low and watching.

LENS & EXPOSURE:
- Focal range: 24mm to 85mm across the sequence.
- Wides: 24–35mm, deeper DOF, slight vignette.
- Close-ups: 85mm, shallow DOF, natural bokeh on entity behind.
- Shutter feel: cinematic 180-degree — controlled, no motion blur excess.
- Exposure: slightly underexposed overall (-1/3 stop) to preserve shadow density.

LIGHT & COLOR:
- Primary grade: cold blue-grey, desaturated skin tones, teal shadows.
- Contrast: high — lifted blacks only in fog glow area.
- Subject A's face: slight warm practical spill to separate him from the cold environment — he is still alive, still human.
- Entity: no warm tones. Pure cold. Eyes rendered in overexposed white-blue.
- Grain: subtle 16mm organic grain layer across all frames.

[KF 2 | 2.5 SEC | MS — INTERIOR DRIVER]

- CAMERA: Slightly low angle from passenger footwell position, angled up 15 degrees. Micro handheld drift — barely perceptible.

[KF 4 | 3 SEC | CU — TERROR FACE]
- COMPOSITION: Subject A in tight close-up, face dominant. Eyes fully wide, whites visible above iris — genuine shock response. Mouth fractionally open. Right frame edge clips his shoulder. Rear window now clearly in background left — entity fully visible, standing, glowing eyes burning through fog, closer now.
- ACTION & BEAT: Full revelation. He sees it. This is the TURN. He does not scream. He cannot move.
- CAMERA: Locked static. No movement. The stillness of the camera amplifies the horror.
- LENS & DOF: 85mm, very shallow DOF, razor focus on Subject A's eyes. Entity in background is soft but unmistakably present — two bright eye-points in the blur.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Slight desaturation push on skin. Cold light rakes across cheekbone. Deep shadow under chin and left jaw. Entity's eyes slightly overexposed — white-blue flare.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Complete silence. Then a single, distant breath — origin unclear.

[KF 5 | 2.5 SEC | ECU — ENTITY EYES THROUGH GLASS]
- COMPOSITION: Extreme close-up of the rear windshield glass surface. The entity's two glowing white eyes centered in frame. Glass texture visible — subtle condensation, fine scratches, the physical barrier between. Entity body barely suggested in dark fog behind. Subject A's headrest blurs in extreme foreground left.
- ACTION & BEAT: The eyes do not blink. They simply exist. They step imperceptibly closer — the glow intensifies by 10%. PAYOFF begins to build.
- CAMERA: Shooting from inside car toward rear glass. Locked static. 2% imperceptible push toward glass.
- LENS & DOF: 85–100mm macro-adjacent, extremely shallow DOF, focus on the glass surface and eye-glow beyond. Foreground headrest fully blurred.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Frame almost entirely cold and dark. The eyes are the only light source in this frame. Grade pushed to near-monochrome with cyan shadows. Grain elevated slightly.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: A low glass resonance — as if something presses from outside.

[KF 6 | 3 SEC | LOW ANGLE WIDE — INTERIOR ENTRAPMENT]
- COMPOSITION: Low worm's-eye angle from below dashboard looking up and back. Full cabin visible — Subject A in driver seat upper right, both rear windows in frame, fog pressing against every pane of glass. Entity silhouette now visible in BOTH rear quarter windows — or its shadow splits across both. The car feels like a cage. Subject A's head is slightly bowed, hand still on wheel.
- ACTION & BEAT: PAYOFF. He is surrounded. The car offers no protection. He is trapped inside his own vehicle with something that does not need a door.
- CAMERA: Ultra-low angle, nearly floor-level, wide. Slow 10-degree lateral arc left — barely moving, like something circling beneath.
- LENS & DOF: 24mm, medium-deep DOF, full interior sharp, fog exterior slightly soft.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Cold fog glow wraps all windows equally — the outside is one continuous threat. Subject A's face in upper frame receives only spill — isolated, diminished. Full teal-black grade. Grain visible.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Fog silence. Then — a single tap on glass. Precise. Deliberate.

- TURN: He sees it clearly — glowing eyes staring back, motionless, patient.
- PAYOFF: The entity steps closer through the fog; the man cannot move. The car is no longer a shelter.

---

C) CINEMATIC APPROACH

SHOT PROGRESSION STRATEGY:
Begin wide to establish the vehicle and fog environment (isolation). Move into a medium on the driver (humanity, vulnerability). Cut to a rear-facing angle revealing the entity (the turn). Push into close-up on Subject A's face (terror internalized). ECU of the glowing eyes through glass (the horror made concrete). End on a low-angle wide inside the car as fog presses against every window (entrapment, no escape).

CAMERA MOVEMENT PLAN:
- KF1: Slow push-in from exterior — clinical, inevitable approach.
- KF2: Locked off or micro-handheld drift — false sense of normalcy disrupted.
- KF3: Very slow pull-back inside cabin — space begins to feel smaller.
- KF4: Static, locked — the horror needs no movement to land.
- KF5: Imperceptible 2% push toward rear window glass — narrowing the world.
- KF6: Low-angle slow arc — 10-degree lateral creep, the perspective of something low and watching.

LENS & EXPOSURE:
- Focal range: 24mm to 85mm across the sequence.
- Wides: 24–35mm, deeper DOF, slight vignette.
- Close-ups: 85mm, shallow DOF, natural bokeh on entity behind.
- Shutter feel: cinematic 180-degree — controlled, no motion blur excess.
- Exposure: slightly underexposed overall (-1/3 stop) to preserve shadow density.

LIGHT & COLOR:
- Primary grade: cold blue-grey, desaturated skin tones, teal shadows.
- Contrast: high — lifted blacks only in fog glow area.
- Subject A's face: slight warm practical spill to separate him from the cold environment — he is still alive, still human.
- Entity: no warm tones. Pure cold. Eyes rendered in overexposed white-blue.
- Grain: subtle 16mm organic grain layer across all frames.

---

D) 6 KEYFRAMES

[KF 1 | 3 SEC | ELS — EXTERIOR WIDE]
- COMPOSITION: Full exterior shot of the stationary or slow-moving vehicle on a fog-choked road. Car centered, road lines converge to black void ahead. Fog swallows the background completely. No visible entity yet — just the car alone in the mist. Trees or guardrails barely suggested in periphery.
- ACTION & BEAT: The car sits in fog. Nothing moves. The stillness is suffocating. SETUP beat — isolation established.
- CAMERA: Eye-level, locked off. Extremely slow 3% push-in toward rear of vehicle. Fog drifts subtly.
- LENS & DOF: 24mm, deep focus, full environment sharp, slight natural vignette.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Cold blue-grey exterior. Fog self-illuminated with ambient night glow. No hard light sources. Taillights faintly red — only warm note in frame.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Low engine idle, distant wind, silence beneath it all.

[KF 2 | 2.5 SEC | MS — INTERIOR DRIVER]
- COMPOSITION: Subject A in medium shot, occupying right two-thirds of frame. Steering wheel in lower foreground. Rear seats and fog-filled rear window visible in left background — entity NOT yet visible. Driver's gaze is forward, expression neutral but slightly tense.
- ACTION & BEAT: Subject A drives. His jaw tightens almost imperceptibly. Something in his peripheral vision registers — he hasn't looked yet. BUILD begins.
- CAMERA: Slightly low angle from passenger footwell position, angled up 15 degrees. Micro handheld drift — barely perceptible.
- LENS & DOF: 35mm, medium DOF, focus on Subject A's face, rear window softly bokeh'd.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Cold ambient fill. Slight warm instrument glow on lower face. Deep shadow on left side. Consistent teal-blue grade.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Subtle tire hum, then silence — the engine seems to hold its breath.

[KF 3 | 2 SEC | MCU — DRIVER REACTION]
- COMPOSITION: Subject A tighter — MCU from chest up. Head now turned slightly toward rearview mirror (off-left). Eyes widened, beginning to process. Rear window visible in background — entity silhouette starts to materialize in fog, glowing eyes just barely present, soft and distant.
- ACTION & BEAT: He sees something. Not fully — just enough. The BUILD peaks. His knuckles whiten on the wheel.
- CAMERA: Same interior position, slight slow push-in 4%. Camera holds axis.
- LENS & DOF: 50mm, shallow DOF, crisp focus on Subject A's eyes and brow, entity behind in soft bokeh — glowing eyes just two blurred white orbs.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Face lit cold. Entity backlit by fog glow. Grade consistent — shadows deepened in upper corners of frame.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: A low sub-frequency hum begins — felt more than heard.

[KF 4 | 3 SEC | CU — TERROR FACE]
- COMPOSITION: Subject A in tight close-up, face dominant. Eyes fully wide, whites visible above iris — genuine shock response. Mouth fractionally open. Right frame edge clips his shoulder. Rear window now clearly in background left — entity fully visible, standing, glowing eyes burning through fog, closer now.
- ACTION & BEAT: Full revelation. He sees it. This is the TURN. He does not scream. He cannot move.
- CAMERA: Locked static. No movement. The stillness of the camera amplifies the horror.
- LENS & DOF: 85mm, very shallow DOF, razor focus on Subject A's eyes. Entity in background is soft but unmistakably present — two bright eye-points in the blur.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Slight desaturation push on skin. Cold light rakes across cheekbone. Deep shadow under chin and left jaw. Entity's eyes slightly overexposed — white-blue flare.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Complete silence. Then a single, distant breath — origin unclear.

[KF 5 | 2.5 SEC | ECU — ENTITY EYES THROUGH GLASS]
- COMPOSITION: Extreme close-up of the rear windshield glass surface. The entity's two glowing white eyes centered in frame. Glass texture visible — subtle condensation, fine scratches, the physical barrier between. Entity body barely suggested in dark fog behind. Subject A's headrest blurs in extreme foreground left.
- ACTION & BEAT: The eyes do not blink. They simply exist. They step imperceptibly closer — the glow intensifies by 10%. PAYOFF begins to build.
- CAMERA: Shooting from inside car toward rear glass. Locked static. 2% imperceptible push toward glass.
- LENS & DOF: 85–100mm macro-adjacent, extremely shallow DOF, focus on the glass surface and eye-glow beyond. Foreground headrest fully blurred.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Frame almost entirely cold and dark. The eyes are the only light source in this frame. Grade pushed to near-monochrome with cyan shadows. Grain elevated slightly.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: A low glass resonance — as if something presses from outside.

[KF 6 | 3 SEC | LOW ANGLE WIDE — INTERIOR ENTRAPMENT]
- COMPOSITION: Low worm's-eye angle from below dashboard looking up and back. Full cabin visible — Subject A in driver seat upper right, both rear windows in frame, fog pressing against every pane of glass. Entity silhouette now visible in BOTH rear quarter windows — or its shadow splits across both. The car feels like a cage. Subject A's head is slightly bowed, hand still on wheel.
- ACTION & BEAT: PAYOFF. He is surrounded. The car offers no protection. He is trapped inside his own vehicle with something that does not need a door.
- CAMERA: Ultra-low angle, nearly floor-level, wide. Slow 10-degree lateral arc left — barely moving, like something circling beneath.
- LENS & DOF: 24mm, medium-deep DOF, full interior sharp, fog exterior slightly soft.
- LIGHTING & GRADE: Cold fog glow wraps all windows equally — the outside is one continuous threat. Subject A's face in upper frame receives only spill — isolated, diminished. Full teal-black grade. Grain visible.
- SOUND & ATMOSPHERE: Fog silence. Then — a single tap on glass. Precise. Deliberate.

---

E) CONTACT SHEET — 2x3 MASTER GRID DESCRIPTION

Generate a single cinematic contact sheet image arranged in a 2-column by 3-row grid as follows:

- PANEL 1 (top-left): KF1 | ELS | 3s — Exterior fog road, vehicle centered, no entity, cold blue-grey, deep focus, fog consuming background.
- PANEL 2 (top-right): KF2 | MS | 2.5s — Interior driver medium shot, Subject A facing forward, neutral tension, rear window empty but fog present, micro-handheld feel.
- PANEL 3 (mid-left): KF3 | MCU | 2s — Subject A head turned toward mirror, eyes beginning to widen, entity silhouette faint and soft in background bokeh, glowing eyes barely visible.
- PANEL 4 (mid-right): KF4 | CU | 3s — Subject A's face in tight close-up, full terror expression, eyes wide, entity clearly present and glowing in shallow background, locked camera.
- PANEL 5 (bottom-left): KF5 | ECU | 2.5s — Extreme close-up of rear windshield glass, two glowing white eyes centered, near-monochrome grade, glass condensation texture visible.
- PANEL 6 (bottom-right): KF6 | LOW WIDE | 3s — Worm's-eye interior wide, Subject A diminished in upper frame, fog surrounding all windows, entity shadow split across rear quarters, slow arc movement.

All panels share: identical dark car interior, same Subject A wardrobe and appearance, consistent cold teal-blue grade, organic 16mm grain, and the same entity with white-glowing eyes. Labels appear in safe margin zones at bottom of each panel: KF number, shot type, duration. No label obscures subject faces or entity eyes.

<ROLE>
YOU ARE A VETERAN SHORT FILM DIRECTOR, CINEMATOGRAPHER, AND STORYBOARD SUPERVISOR. YOUR MISSION: TAKE ONE REFERENCE IMAGE AND ONE MOOD DESCRIPTION AND TRANSFORM THEM INTO A PRODUCTION-READY 6-KEYFRAME CINEMATIC SEQUENCE BUILT FOR AI VIDEO GENERATION.
</ROLE>


<INPUT>
USER PROVIDES: ONE REFERENCE IMAGE + ONE TEXT INPUT DESCRIBING THE MOOD OF THE SHORT FILM.
</INPUT>


<CONTEXT>
THE USER WILL PROVIDE 1 SINGLE IMAGE AS A VISUAL REFERENCE FOR THE ENTIRE SEQUENCE AND 1 TEXT INPUT DESCRIBING THE MOOD OF THE SHORT FILM. YOUR JOB IS TO DEEPLY ANALYZE THE IMAGE AND USE THE MOOD AS THE EMOTIONAL FILTER THAT SHAPES EVERY DECISION — FROM COLOR AND LIGHTING TO CAMERA MOVEMENT AND NARRATIVE ARC. THE MOOD MUST INFECT EVERY KEYFRAME, EVERY SHOT CHOICE, AND EVERY ATMOSPHERIC DETAIL. DO NOT ASK FOR ADDITIONAL INPUT. ANALYZE BOTH AND BEGIN IMMEDIATELY.
</CONTEXT>


<NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES — CONTINUITY & TRUTHFULNESS>
1.⁠ ⁠START BY READING THE ENTIRE FRAME: IDENTIFY EVERY KEY SUBJECT (PERSON / GROUP / OBJECT / VEHICLE / ANIMAL / PROPS / ENVIRONMENTAL ELEMENTS). DESCRIBE THEIR SPATIAL RELATIONSHIPS, POSITIONS (LEFT/RIGHT/FOREGROUND/BACKGROUND), FACING DIRECTION, CURRENT ACTION, AND HOW THEY INTERACT WITH EACH OTHER.
2.⁠ ⁠NEVER FABRICATE REAL IDENTITIES, REAL LOCATION NAMES, OR BRAND AFFILIATIONS. WORK ONLY WITH WHAT IS VISIBLE IN THE IMAGE. EMOTIONAL AND ATMOSPHERIC INTERPRETATION IS PERMITTED — FACTUAL INVENTION IS NOT.
3.⁠ ⁠ABSOLUTE VISUAL CONTINUITY ACROSS ALL 6 SHOTS: SAME SUBJECTS, SAME WARDROBE, SAME PHYSICAL APPEARANCE, SAME ENVIRONMENT, SAME TIME OF DAY, SAME LIGHTING STYLE. ONLY FRAMING, BLOCKING, EXPRESSION, ANGLE, AND CAMERA BEHAVIOR MAY CHANGE BETWEEN SHOTS.
4.⁠ ⁠DEPTH OF FIELD MUST FOLLOW OPTICAL LOGIC: WIDER SHOTS CARRY DEEPER FOCUS, CLOSE-UPS CARRY NATURAL LENS SEPARATION WITH ORGANIC BOKEH. ONE UNIFIED CINEMATIC COLOR GRADE MUST RUN ACROSS THE ENTIRE SEQUENCE.
5.⁠ ⁠DO NOT ADD NEW SUBJECTS, OBJECTS, OR STORY ELEMENTS THAT ARE ABSENT FROM THE REFERENCE IMAGE. IF THE NARRATIVE REQUIRES TENSION OR CONFLICT, SUGGEST IT THROUGH OFF-SCREEN MEANS — SHADOW, REFLECTION, GAZE, SOUND, OR OCCLUSION. NEVER MANUFACTURE IT.
</NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES — CONTINUITY & TRUTHFULNESS>


<GOAL>
USING THE REFERENCE IMAGE AND THE MOOD INPUT, BUILD A 6-KEYFRAME CINEMATIC SEQUENCE THAT COVERS 10 TO 20 SECONDS OF SCREEN TIME WITH A CLEAR EMOTIONAL JOURNEY: SETUP → BUILD → TURN → PAYOFF. EACH KEYFRAME WILL BE USED DIRECTLY FOR AI VIDEO GENERATION AND STITCHED INTO A FINAL CUT BY THE USER. EACH FRAME SHOULD BE UNIQUE AND DIFERENT.
</GOAL>


⸻


<STEP 1 — SCENE BREAKDOWN>


OUTPUT WITH CLEAR SUBHEADINGS:


•⁠  ⁠SUBJECTS: LABEL EACH KEY SUBJECT (A / B / C...). FOR EACH ONE DESCRIBE: VISIBLE PHYSICAL TRAITS AND WARDROBE, POSITION IN THE FRAME, FACING DIRECTION, CURRENT ACTION OR STATE, AND RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER SUBJECTS.


•⁠  ⁠ENVIRONMENT & LIGHTING: INTERIOR OR EXTERIOR, SPATIAL SCALE AND LAYOUT, BACKGROUND ELEMENTS, SURFACE MATERIALS AND TEXTURES, LIGHT DIRECTION AND QUALITY (HARD OR SOFT / KEY FILL RIM), IMPLIED TIME OF DAY, AND 3 TO 8 ATMOSPHERE KEYWORDS THAT DEFINE THE EMOTIONAL REGISTER OF THE SPACE.


•⁠  ⁠VISUAL ANCHORS: IDENTIFY 3 TO 6 SPECIFIC VISUAL CONSTANTS THAT MUST REMAIN IDENTICAL ACROSS ALL 6 SHOTS — FOR EXAMPLE: A DOMINANT COLOR, A RECURRING PROP, THE PRIMARY LIGHT SOURCE, A WEATHER CONDITION, A FILM TEXTURE, OR A BACKGROUND LANDMARK.


•⁠  ⁠MOOD INTEGRATION: DESCRIBE HOW THE USER-PROVIDED MOOD INPUT WILL SHAPE THE VISUAL DECISIONS OF THE SEQUENCE — COLOR TEMPERATURE, SHADOW DEPTH, CAMERA BEHAVIOR, PACING, AND EMOTIONAL REGISTER.
</STEP 1 — SCENE BREAKDOWN>


⸻


<STEP 2 — THEME & STORY>


DERIVE THE NARRATIVE FROM THE IMAGE AND THE MOOD. OUTPUT:


•⁠  ⁠THEME: ONE SENTENCE NAMING THE EMOTIONAL OR PHILOSOPHICAL CORE OF THIS SEQUENCE.
•⁠  ⁠LOGLINE: ONE RESTRAINED TRAILER-STYLE SENTENCE GROUNDED ONLY IN WHAT THE IMAGE AND MOOD CAN SUPPORT.
•⁠  ⁠EMOTIONAL ARC — 4 BEATS, ONE LINE EACH:
  - SETUP: THE OPENING EMOTIONAL STATE.
  - BUILD: THE RISING TENSION OR MOMENTUM.
  - TURN: THE SHIFT OR REVELATION.
  - PAYOFF: THE FINAL EMOTIONAL LANDING.
</STEP 2 — THEME & STORY>


⸻


<STEP 3 — CINEMATIC APPROACH>


DEFINE THE VISUAL LANGUAGE OF THE SEQUENCE. MUST ADDRESS ALL FOUR AREAS:


•⁠  ⁠SHOT PROGRESSION STRATEGY: HOW YOU MOVE THROUGH FOCAL LENGTHS AND DISTANCES ACROSS THE 6 SHOTS TO SERVE EACH EMOTIONAL BEAT.
•⁠  ⁠CAMERA MOVEMENT PLAN: SPECIFY EVERY MOVEMENT YOU WILL USE — PUSH / PULL / PAN / DOLLY / TRACK / ORBIT / HANDHELD / GIMBAL — AND EXPLAIN THE INTENTION BEHIND EACH.
•⁠  ⁠LENS & EXPOSURE: RECOMMENDED FOCAL LENGTH RANGE, DEPTH OF FIELD TENDENCY, AND OVERALL SHUTTER FEEL — CINEMATIC AND CONTROLLED VERSUS DOCUMENTARY AND RAW.
•⁠  ⁠LIGHT & COLOR: CONTRAST LEVEL, KEY TONES, HOW MATERIALS SHOULD RENDER, WHETHER GRAIN IS APPROPRIATE. EVERYTHING MUST FEEL CONSISTENT WITH THE REFERENCE IMAGE AND CHARGED WITH THE USER-PROVIDED MOOD.
</STEP 3 — CINEMATIC APPROACH>


⸻


<STEP 4 — 6 KEYFRAMES FOR AI VIDEO (PRIMARY DELIVERABLE)>


OUTPUT EXACTLY 6 KEYFRAMES THAT FORM A COHERENT 10 TO 20 SECOND SEQUENCE FOLLOWING THE 4-BEAT EMOTIONAL ARC. EVERY FRAME SHOULD CONTAIN UNIQUE ACTION AND SHOULD NOT BE EQUAL TO ANOTHER PANEL. MUST BE A BELIEVABLE CONTINUATION WITHIN THE SAME ENVIRONMENT AS THE REFERENCE IMAGE. THE MOOD MUST BE LEGIBLE IN EVERY SINGLE FRAME.


USE THIS EXACT FORMAT FOR EACH KEYFRAME:


[KF # | DURATION (SEC) | SHOT TYPE: ELS / LS / MLS / MS / MCU / CU / ECU / LOW / WORMS-EYE / HIGH / BIRDS-EYE / INSERT]
•⁠  ⁠COMPOSITION: SUBJECT PLACEMENT IN FRAME, WHAT OCCUPIES FOREGROUND MID AND BACKGROUND, LEADING LINES, GAZE DIRECTION.
•⁠  ⁠ACTION & BEAT: WHAT PHYSICALLY HAPPENS IN THIS FRAME. KEEP IT SIMPLE AND EXECUTABLE.
•⁠  ⁠CAMERA: HEIGHT, ANGLE, AND MOVEMENT — DESCRIBED PRECISELY. EXAMPLE: SLOW 5% PUSH-IN / 1M LATERAL DOLLY / SUBTLE HANDHELD DRIFT.
•⁠  ⁠LENS & DOF: FOCAL LENGTH IN MM, DEPTH OF FIELD (SHALLOW / MEDIUM / DEEP), FOCUS TARGET.
•⁠  ⁠LIGHTING & GRADE: MAINTAIN CONSISTENCY WITH THE ESTABLISHED GRADE. FLAG ANY HIGHLIGHT OR SHADOW EMPHASIS SPECIFIC TO THIS FRAME.
•⁠  ⁠SOUND & ATMOSPHERE (OPTIONAL): ONE LINE OF AMBIENT OR DIEGETIC SOUND THAT SUPPORTS THE EDIT RHYTHM OF THIS FRAME.


HARD REQUIREMENTS:
•⁠  ⁠THE 6 KEYFRAMES MUST INCLUDE AT MINIMUM: 1 ENVIRONMENT-ESTABLISHING WIDE SHOT, 1 INTIMATE CLOSE-UP, 1 EXTREME DETAIL ECU, AND 1 POWER-ANGLE SHOT (LOW OR HIGH ANGLE).
•⁠  ⁠SHOTS MUST BE EDIT-MOTIVATED: MAINTAIN EYELINE MATCHES, ACTION CONTINUITY, AND CONSISTENT SCREEN DIRECTION ACROSS THE AXIS THROUGHOUT THE SEQUENCE.
</STEP 4 — 6 KEYFRAMES FOR AI VIDEO>


⸻


<STEP 5 — CONTACT SHEET OUTPUT>


OUTPUT ONE SINGLE MASTER IMAGE: A CINEMATIC CONTACT SHEET CONTAINING ALL 6 KEYFRAMES ARRANGED IN A 2-COLUMN BY 3-ROW GRID (2X3).


REQUIREMENTS:
1.⁠ ⁠EVERY KEYFRAME APPEARS AS ITS OWN PANEL — ONE SHOT PER CELL. NO KEYFRAME MAY BE OMITTED.
2.⁠ ⁠EACH PANEL MUST BE LABELED WITH: KF NUMBER + SHOT TYPE + SUGGESTED DURATION. LABELS SIT IN SAFE MARGIN AREAS AND MUST NEVER OBSCURE THE SUBJECT.
3.⁠ ⁠ALL PANELS MUST REFLECT THE SAME SUBJECTS, WARDROBE, ENVIRONMENT, LIGHTING, AND COLOR GRADE. ONLY ACTION, EXPRESSION, BLOCKING, FRAMING, AND CAMERA BEHAVIOR MAY DIFFER BETWEEN PANELS. MAKE SURE ACTION IS DIFFERENT IN EACH PANEL.
4.⁠ ⁠DEPTH OF FIELD SHIFTS LOGICALLY ACROSS PANELS: SHALLOW IN CLOSE-UPS, DEEPER IN WIDES. TEXTURES MUST BE PHOTOREALISTIC AND GRADING CONSISTENT ACROSS ALL CELLS.
5.⁠ ⁠AFTER THE MASTER GRID IMAGE, OUTPUT THE COMPLETE WRITTEN BREAKDOWN FOR ALL 6 KEYFRAMES IN NUMBERED ORDER SO THE USER CAN REGENERATE ANY INDIVIDUAL FRAME AT HIGHER RESOLUTION.
</STEP 5 — CONTACT SHEET OUTPUT>


⸻


<FINAL OUTPUT ORDER>
A) SCENE BREAKDOWN
B) THEME & STORY
C) CINEMATIC APPROACH
D) 6 KEYFRAMES LIST
E) ONE 2X3 MASTER CONTACT SHEET IMAGE
</FINAL OUTPUT ORDER>

You are a portrait re-posing specialist. Your task is to take the provided reference image of a person facing the camera head-on (front-facing headshot) and generate a new image of the SAME person, turned to {{ANGLE}}.

{{ANGLE}} = 90 clockwise

Critical rules:

1. POSE ROTATION, NOT IMAGE ROTATION: Do NOT rotate, skew, or transform the image canvas itself. Instead, realistically re-render the subject's head, neck, shoulders, and upper body as they would naturally appear when the person has turned their body and head to {{ANGLE}}. The camera stays fixed in place; only the person moves.

2. ANGLE INTERPRETATION: Treat {{ANGLE}} as the horizontal (yaw) rotation of the subject relative to the camera.
   - 0° = facing directly toward camera (front)
   - 45° left = three-quarter view, head turned left
   - 90° left = full left profile
   - 135° left = three-quarter back, turned left
   - 180° = back of head facing camera
   - Negative or right values mirror accordingly (e.g., 45° right = three-quarter view turned right)

3. IDENTITY PRESERVATION: Maintain the exact same person — same skin tone, facial structure, hair texture, hair length, hair color, and hairstyle. Preserve every accessory (hats, jewelry, glasses) and clothing (fabric, color, fit, collar shape, layering) exactly as shown in the reference.

4. ANATOMICAL ACCURACY AT {{ANGLE}}: Reconstruct what would realistically be visible at {{ANGLE}}. For example:
   - At a three-quarter view, one ear becomes visible, the far eye appears slightly narrower, the nose bridges across the midline of the face, and the jawline foreshortens on the far side.
   - At a full profile (90°), only one eye is visible, the ear is fully exposed, and the nose extends past the silhouette of the face.
   - At rear angles (beyond 90°), progressively less of the face is visible; the back of the head, hair, nape, and rear contours of clothing become dominant.
   - Hair should fall and drape naturally for {{ANGLE}}, accounting for gravity and how it would shift with the head turn.
   - Hats and headwear must sit on the head correctly and be shown from the perspective consistent with {{ANGLE}}.

5. LIGHTING AND BACKGROUND CONSISTENCY: Keep the same flat, clean, neutral background (white/light gray). Maintain the same soft, even, studio-style lighting. Shadows and highlights on the face and clothing should update naturally to reflect the new orientation at {{ANGLE}} while preserving the same overall lighting mood.

6. FRAMING AND COMPOSITION: Keep the same tight crop — head and upper torso centered in frame. The subject should remain at the same scale and vertical position. Do not zoom in or out. The image dimensions and aspect ratio must stay the same as the original.

7. EXPRESSION: If the face is visible at {{ANGLE}}, maintain a neutral, calm expression consistent with the reference photo. Do not add smiles, squints, or any emotional shift.

8. PHOTOREALISM: The output must be indistinguishable from a real studio photograph. No painterly effects, no AI artifacts, no warping. Skin texture, fabric weave, hair strands — all must hold up at high resolution.

Your single input variable is {{ANGLE}}. Every instruction above adapts to whatever value is placed in {{ANGLE}}. Simply replace {{ANGLE}} with your desired orientation (e.g., 45° left, 90° right, 180°, slight 15° left tilt, etc.) and the prompt governs the entire generation accordingly.

Final look should feel like a frame pulled from a Bong Joon-ho or Roger Deakins production — precise, emotionally loaded, and achingly cinematic.

Color temperature should be used as an emotional instrument: push cooler (5500K–6500K) for psychological distance and melancholy, and warmer (2700K–3200K) for vulnerability and intimacy. Introduce a faint cyan-turquoise wash in underexposed areas to evoke mercury vapor or underwater stillness. Skin tones should lean peachy-beige with subtle olive undertones, never oversaturated. Contrast ratios should be high and deliberate — compress the upper two-thirds of the frame toward darkness when composing for isolation, and allow a single warm or cool light source to define the subject. Add a complementary teal-amber split tone in the color wheels, with teal seated in the shadows and amber warming the midtones. Final look should feel like a frame pulled from a Bong Joon-ho or Roger Deakins production — precise, emotionally loaded, and achingly cinematic.

01c9a737-da72-461a-9d04-a96239a8fbb2.text:
Lighting Breakdown — Soft Frontal Daylight Portrait

- Overall read: One large, soft, slightly frontal-left source with gentle falloff. Shadow under the nose and chin is short and soft, catchlights sit high and wide — classic north-facing window or a big diffused source close to the subject.

1. Key light
   - Source: 4x6 ft window with sheer diffusion, or a 5-7 ft octabox / scrim frame with a 650-1000W tungsten or 300-600Ws strobe pushed through.
   - Position: camera-left, roughly 15-25° off axis, raised just above eye level (butterfly-leaning-loop). Tilted slightly down.
   - Distance: close — 3 to 4 ft from the face. This is what creates the creamy skin transition and the soft wrap around the cheekbone.
   - Quality: heavily diffused, no grid. You want the source larger than the subject's head by a wide margin.

2. Fill
   - A white V-flat or 4x4 foam board camera-right, 2-3 ft away, feathered back.
   - Ratio around 2:1 to 2.5:1 — shadows stay open, never black, but the right side of the face still recedes.

3. Background
   - Plain warm-grey / off-white wall, subject placed 2-4 ft in front of it.
   - No dedicated background light. The soft key spills naturally, producing that faint darker gradient upper-right and the barely-there shadow edge behind the shoulder. That soft shadow confirms a single source, not a multi-light setup.

4. Negative fill
   - Optional black flag low and camera-right to keep the jawline and neck from flattening out, and to preserve separation between dark hair and the wall.

5. Camera and exposure
   - 85mm to 105mm equivalent, shot at eye level, dead-on for that direct, unposed gaze.
   - f/2.8-f/4 to keep facial features sharp while the wall stays smooth.
   - ISO 400-800 on film or a mild grain emulation — the texture here reads like 35mm Portra or a low-contrast digital profile.

6. Grade and finish
   - Lifted blacks, desaturated neutrals, slight cool-grey cast in the wall against warm skin.
   - Minimal retouching — freckles and pores are the point. Keep the specular highlights on the lips and nose bridge intact.

Simplest real-world version: sit her a few feet from a big north window on an overcast day, bounce card on the opposite side, shoot at eye level. That's the whole setup.

Smooth, gradual highlight-to-shadow transitions across the cheeks, nose, and jawline. A faint, delicate nose shadow drifting softly toward the shadow side. The shadow side of the face remains open and detailed with lifted tones, never going dark or hollow. Subtle restored contrast along the lower jawline and neck to preserve clean facial definition. Broad, creamy highlights on the forehead, nose bridge, and cheekbones with no harsh specular edges. Skin rendered smooth and flattering with softened texture and natural tonal evenness. Eyes bright and engaged with a large, soft catchlight positioned slightly above center in the iris on the key side. Hair showing a restrained, gentle sheen on the lit side and slightly denser tonality on the fill side, with no rim light. Low-to-medium overall contrast, quietly dimensional, never flat and never dramatic. Light quality that feels natural, intimate, refined, and subtly editorial, as if lit by a very large, close, diffused source just off axis. No visible hard-edged shadows on the background or subject.

e7e02e8b-d08c-4633-93ed-430dc4348800.text:
- This is a controlled, minimalist portrait setup built to create soft, directional light with gentle shaping, subtle contrast, and a very clean background separation without looking flashy or obviously lit. It is designed for a natural, modern headshot or beauty portrait where the lighting feels refined rather than dramatic.

- Core structure of the setup:
  - A seamless backdrop is placed behind the subject.
  - The subject stands or sits roughly 2 to 4 feet in front of that backdrop.
  - The camera is directly in front of the subject, on axis, at eye level.
  - The key light is camera left, placed about 15 to 25 degrees off axis and about 3 to 4 feet from the subject.
  - The key is raised slightly above the subject and angled downward toward the face.
  - The modifier is a large octabox, roughly 5 to 7 feet, which makes the source broad and wrapping.
  - On camera right, a large white V-flat acts as passive fill, bouncing some of the key light back into the shadow side of the face.
  - Near the lower camera-right jaw and shoulder area, a black flag provides negative fill, selectively subtracting some of that bounced light so the portrait does not become too flat.

- What each element is doing:
  - Seamless backdrop:
    - Creates a distraction-free field behind the subject.
    - Because the subject is several feet away from it, the background receives less direct spill and stays smoother and slightly separated tonally.
    - The distance helps reduce harsh shadows falling onto the backdrop.
    - The result is a soft, nearly uniform background with a faint natural gradient rather than a hard-lit wall.

  - Subject 2 to 4 feet off the background:
    - This spacing is extremely important.
    - It prevents the portrait from looking cramped or amateurishly pinned to the wall.
    - It allows the key light to shape the face without strongly shaping the backdrop.
    - It improves tonal separation, even if the wardrobe is dark and the background is light.
    - If depth of field is moderate, the backdrop also softens slightly, making the image feel more polished.

  - Camera on axis at eye level:
    - Keeps perspective natural and neutral.
    - Makes the portrait feel direct, honest, and calm.
    - Avoids the dominance of a low angle or the vulnerability of a high angle.
    - Maintains symmetry in the framing, which pairs well with the soft asymmetry of the lighting.

  - Large octabox as key light:
    - This is the defining tool in the setup.
    - A 5 to 7 foot octabox is huge relative to a head-and-shoulders subject.
    - Because it is also fairly close, the apparent size of the source is very large.
    - Large apparent size means soft transition edges, broad wrap, and flattering skin rendering.
    - The octagonal shape tends to create attractive rounded catchlights, though in practice they may appear almost window-like because of diffusion.
    - The front diffusion spreads light evenly across the face, reducing harsh micro-shadows.

  - Key light placement at 15 to 25 degrees off axis:
    - This is a very subtle side placement, not a dramatic side light.
    - It keeps the face mostly frontal while still introducing direction.
    - The result is gentle modeling across the cheeks, nose, lips, and jaw.
    - It avoids the flatness of pure on-axis light while also avoiding the severity of a 45-degree Rembrandt-style setup.
    - This angle is ideal for clean editorial, beauty, fashion basics, and straightforward portraiture.

  - Key light raised and angled down:
    - This imitates a natural top-front light direction, similar to a soft skylight or high window.
    - It helps form a mild shadow under the brow, nose, lower lip, and chin.
    - Because the source is large, these shadows remain diffused and elegant rather than sharp.
    - The downward angle sculpts the face slightly, which keeps the portrait from feeling like flat passport lighting.

  - White V-flat on camera right:
    - This catches spill from the key and returns it into the shadow side.
    - It opens up density in the far cheek, jawline, neck, and hair.
    - It preserves detail in the dark side of the face while maintaining a very soft rolloff.
    - Because it is a passive bounce, the fill is naturally weaker and softer than the key.
    - It contributes to the airy, clean, contemporary feeling of the portrait.

  - Black flag low on camera right:
    - This is the subtle sophistication move in the setup.
    - Without it, the V-flat might overfill the lower shadow side and reduce facial definition.
    - By placing black negative fill near the jaw and shoulder zone, some of the stray bounce is absorbed.
    - This restores contour along the lower face and neck.
    - It helps the jawline read more cleanly.
    - It can also keep dark clothing from lifting too much in exposure, preserving richness and shape.

- The lighting pattern it creates on the face:
  - The look is best described as soft short-loop or near-butterfly/loop hybrid, depending on the exact height and angle of the key.
  - Because the key is only modestly off axis, the nose shadow will be small and delicate, likely drifting slightly toward the shadow side rather than dropping straight down.
  - The far cheek will be a little darker than the key side, but not dramatically so because of the V-flat fill.
  - The forehead, nose bridge, cheekbones, and lips will receive smooth, broad highlights.
  - The transitions from highlight to midtone to shadow will be very gradual.
  - There will be enough shape to define bone structure, but not enough to feel theatrical.

- What the light quality feels like visually:
  - Soft, but not flat.
  - Clean, but not clinical.
  - Sculpted, but understated.
  - Natural-looking, but more perfected than actual ambient daylight.
  - Calm, direct, and elegant.

- Contrast characteristics:
  - The key source itself suggests low to medium contrast because it is very large and close.
  - The white V-flat reduces contrast further by lifting the shadow side.
  - The black flag then selectively reintroduces local contrast where needed.
  - So the final image has an overall low-to-medium global contrast, with strategic medium contrast around the jaw, lower cheek, and shoulder.
  - This is why the result feels dimensional without becoming moody.

- Shadow behavior:
  - Nose shadow:
    - Small, soft-edged, unobtrusive.
    - Likely visible, but faint.
  - Under-chin shadow:
    - Present enough to separate chin from neck.
    - Softened by the broad source and some return fill.
  - Cheek shadow:
    - Gentle tonal drop on the side away from the key.
    - The V-flat prevents it from going hollow or severe.
  - Background shadow:
    - Minimal to nearly invisible if distances and feathering are controlled well.
    - Any remaining background gradient will feel soft and natural rather than like a hard cast shadow.

- Highlight behavior:
  - Highlights will be broad and creamy rather than specular and sharp.
  - Skin texture will appear smoother because the large source fills micro-relief in the skin.
  - Forehead and nose highlights should appear soft and elongated.
  - Lips may show a polished, subtle sheen if the subject has natural or styled moisture on the lips.
  - Hair on the key side will pick up a restrained soft sheen, not a crisp rim.

- Catchlights and eye rendering:
  - The eyes will likely have a large, soft catchlight on the key side, positioned slightly above center because the key is raised.
  - Because the light is close to camera axis, the eyes stay bright and engaged.
  - The iris and sclera will not fall off too deeply into shadow.
  - This contributes to a direct, intimate portrait feel.
  - If the fill is strong enough, both eyes will remain very readable with little asymmetry.

- Effect on skin texture and facial features:
  - Large diffusion reduces pore emphasis and minimizes harsh textural contrast.
  - It is flattering for beauty, fashion basics, skincare, and clean editorial portraiture.
  - Fine lines and unevenness are softened, especially compared with smaller or harder sources.
  - The slight off-axis placement still preserves enough form to define cheekbones and nose shape.
  - Freckles or subtle complexion details remain visible, but without being aggressively etched.

- Effect on hair:
  - Dark hair against a pale background will separate primarily through tonal contrast, not rim light.
  - On the key side, the hair may show a soft reflective edge or gentle shine.
  - On the fill side, the hair remains controlled and slightly denser.
  - Because there is no dedicated hair light, the hair rendering stays natural and understated.
  - This avoids a glossy commercial rim-lit look.

- Effect on wardrobe, especially dark clothing:
  - Dark clothing will stay rich and simple.
  - The black flag helps prevent the fill side from becoming washed out or gray.
  - The key side of the garment may show a gentle broad highlight across the shoulder and upper chest.
  - Overall, clothing supports the face rather than competing with it.

- Background rendering:
  - The backdrop will likely appear pale gray to off-white depending on exposure.
  - Since it is not separately lit, it will not blow out to a pure paper white unless the key spills heavily or the exposure is pushed.
  - There may be a very subtle center-to-edge or top-to-bottom gradient caused by light falloff and feathering.
  - This slight tonal variation often feels more expensive and photographic than perfectly flat white.

- Why the result looks modern and refined:
  - The key is close enough to be flattering.
  - The angle is restrained enough to remain approachable.
  - The bounce fill adds openness and polish.
  - The negative fill preserves structure so the image does not become milky.
  - The subject-background distance creates separation without obvious drama.
  - Nothing in the setup screams studio trickery, which is often the hallmark of sophisticated portrait lighting.

- Emotional tone of the lighting:
  - Neutral
  - Intimate
  - Quietly sculptural
  - Honest and direct
  - Slightly editorial
  - Calm rather than energetic
  - Elegant rather than glamorous

- In practical portrait terms, this setup produces:
  - A face that feels softly illuminated from one side/front.
  - A gentle shadow side with retained detail.
  - Softly defined cheekbones and jawline.
  - Eyes that feel open and present.
  - Skin that appears smooth, natural, and flattering.
  - A background that feels clean and separated without needing a dedicated background light.

- If tuned carefully, the final image lands in this sweet spot:
  - More dimensional than flat beauty light
  - Less dramatic than classic side key portraiture
  - More polished than window light alone
  - More natural than high-contrast fashion lighting

- A concise aesthetic summary:
  - Large, close, slightly off-axis key light
  - Gentle downward sculpting
  - Soft bounce fill on the opposite side
  - Selective negative fill to recover shape
  - Clean seamless background with modest subject separation
  - Result: a soft, naturalistic, editorial portrait with smooth skin, delicate shadow modeling, and subtle but intentional facial definition

Create a single 4:3 canvas containing a 2x2 storyboard grid of 4 equal panels with NO borders/gutters/lines between panels (seamless edge-to-edge quadrants). High-end editorial studio series for a designer branding portfolio. Use the reference images as strict anchors.

GLOBAL LOCKS (apply to ALL 4 panels)
- Product lock: EXACT same lipstick as the product reference: identical chrome/silver tube, identical red bullet shape, identical cap form, identical proportions, identical surface finish and reflections. Do not alter the product design in any way. The product must be clearly recognizable in every panel.
- Identity lock: keep branding/labeling exactly as reference (do not invent new logos or text; if the reference has no visible label text, add none). No relocating or retyping any text. No random typography.
- Model lock: Use the model from the portrait reference with the same facial features, expression, skin texture, freckles/flush, makeup look, and hair styling. Do not change identity-defining features. If an edge case results in two models, incorporate BOTH models consistently across the grid (both present in each relevant panel; do not add additional people beyond those two).
- Style lock: curated editorial, design-driven, minimal, calm, confident, studio logic. Consistent neutral studio background language across all panels (soft pale grey/green tint allowed, matching the product reference vibe). Consistent lighting direction, color palette, and visual rhythm across the full 2x2 grid.
- Camera lock: real camera look, ultra-high quality studio photography, controlled depth of field, precise specular highlights on chrome, accurate materials and reflections, no CGI look.
- Composition lock: each panel is self-contained; nothing bleeds/crosses into adjacent panels. No duplicated frames. No collage artifacts.

Panel 1 (top-left): Front-facing hero shot. Product is the main focus. Clean studio setup, neutral background, balanced composition. - No low-res, no blur except intentional motion blur in panel 4, no noise, no compression artifacts, no CGI/plastic look, no over-smoothing.
- No extreme color shifts, no harsh shadows inconsistent with studio lighting, no inconsistent perspective across panels.

Use Image 1 as the only reference for the person's facial features (ignore pose, lighting, camera lens, background, clothing).

Create a clean Apple-style 3D memoji head (like Image 2) from the portrait in Image 1.

Face detection + normalization
- Detect the face in Image 1 and extract identity cues: face shape, hairline, eyebrow shape, eye shape, nose shape, lip shape, ear size/position, facial hair, glasses, piercings, defining marks.
- Rebuild the person as a memoji with simplified, smooth 3D cartoon geometry and soft shading.
- Enforce a fixed, consistent head scale and framing identical to Image 2: centered head, same margin/padding, same apparent head size across all outputs.
- Do not follow the input crop/head size; always match the Image 2 head size and placement.

Background + crop rules
- Background must be pure white (#FFFFFF), flat and uniform.
- Output only the head (no neck, no shoulders, no body).
- Keep the same viewing angle as Image 2: straight-on, neutral, symmetrical, centered.

Memoji style rules (match Image 2)
- Smooth plastic-like 3D material, subtle gradients, soft highlights, no harsh shadows.
- Large expressive eyes, clean outlines, simplified features, friendly neutral expression.
- No photoreal skin texture, no pores, no realistic hair strands; use stylized hair clumps.
- High resolution, crisp edges.

Customizable components (use these variables)
- Hairstyle: medium-length wavy hair with natural volume, side-swept front
- Hair color: very dark brown / near black
- Eyebrows: slightly arched, natural shape
- Brow thickness: medium
- Brow color: dark brown / black
- Eye color: dark brown
- Eye size: medium-large memoji
- Nose size: medium, slightly broad at the base
- Mouth/lip fullness: wide friendly smile showing upper teeth, medium-full lips
- Ear size: medium, partially visible under hair
- Skin tone: warm light-medium tan (light olive/Asian undertone)
- Glasses: off
- Glasses shape: none
- Glasses color: none
- Beard style: clean-shaven / very minimal stubble
- Beard density: none
- Beard color: none
- Mustache style: none
- Piercings: none
- Accessories: none

Identity fidelity priorities
- Prioritize matching: wavy dark hair silhouette, slightly squinting expressive eyes, wide bright smile, defined jawline, warm tan skin tone, clean-shaven face.
- Keep features consistent and coherent in memoji style; avoid uncanny realism.

Negative constraints (do NOT do these)
- No neck/body/clothing.
- No background other than pure white.
- No dramatic lighting, no scene, no bokeh.
- No exaggerated head size variation between different inputs.
- No text, watermark, border, or extra objects.

- Centered memoji head, fixed scale like Image 2, pure white background, clean 3D memoji look.
- If any attribute is unclear from Image 1, choose a neutral default that best matches typical memoji aesthetics while preserving identity.

Final Composition

13. The final layout should feel balanced, breathable, and professionally composed with no dead or awkward negative space.

86b77557-f199-40c4-a9a8-9e8e6262b068.text:
You are a regional localization specialist for graphic design ads. When given any ad image and a target market, your job is to generate a prompt that localizes the graphic for that market. The image itself should remain virtually identical — same model, same pose, same background, same product placement, same layout, same color palette. The only changes should be translating the on-graphic text (headlines, taglines, CTAs, product descriptors) into the language of the target market.

## ANALYSIS STEP (silent — do not output)

When you receive an ad image, identify:
1. Every piece of text visible on the graphic (headlines, subheadlines, taglines, CTAs, body copy, product feature callouts, badges)
2. The current language of the text
3. The brand name, sub-brand names, and proprietary product line names — these stay in English (or their original language) across all markets as they are global brand trademarks

## TRANSLATION RULES

- **KEEP in original language (never translate):** Brand name, sub-brand names, proprietary product line names, trademarked technology names, model/ambassador names, and any other proper nouns that function as global trademarks
- **TRANSLATE into the target language:** Headlines, taglines, body copy, CTAs (e.g., "SHOP NOW"), product feature descriptions, any descriptive or promotional text
- Maintain the same typographic style, weight, size, and placement as the original
- For RTL languages (Arabic, Hebrew), mirror the text direction while preserving the overall graphic layout
- Use the same decorative or script font style where applicable — match the energy of the original typography (e.g., if the original uses a playful script headline, the translation should also be rendered in a playful script style)

## USER INPUT

The user will provide:
1. An ad image
2. One or more target markets (e.g., "Tokyo," "Dubai and São Paulo," "all of Latin America")

If the user provides a broad region (e.g., "Europe"), generate a prompt for each major language market within that region. If the original ad is already in the same language as a requested market, flag this and suggest an alternative.

## OUTPUT FORMAT

Return ONLY the prompt(s), one per market:

**[City] ([Language]):**
Localize this ad graphic for the [City/Market Name] market. Keep the entire graphic identical — same model, same pose, same background, same product placement, same layout, same colors. Only change the text on the graphic to [Language]. Here are the translations:

- "[Original text 1]" → "[Translated text 1]"
- "[Original text 2]" → "[Translated text 2]"
- "[Original text 3]" → "[Translated text 3]"

[Continue for all visible text on the graphic. Keep brand names, sub-brand names, and trademarked product names in their original language.]

No analysis, no rationale, no explanations. Just the production-ready prompt(s) with complete translation tables.

TASK: Using img1 as reference, generate a new headshot photo of the SAME person as if a photographer circled around their head and shot from a new position. The person remains facing naturally with their head upright. The photo stays upright — top of head at top, chin at bottom, always.

CAMERA POSITION: {ANGLE}

{ANGLE} = 45 clockwise

How to interpret {ANGLE}:
- "right profile" or "90 right" = the camera is now at the person's right-hand side. We see a classic side profile: right ear, right jawline closest to camera, nose pointing screen-left. This is a SIDE VIEW, not a tilt.
- "left profile" or "90 left" = camera at the person's left-hand side.
- "3/4 right" or "45 right" = camera between front and right, showing a three-quarter face view.
- "3/4 left" or "45 left" = camera between front and left, showing a three-quarter face view.
- "back" or "180" = camera behind the person, we see the back of their head and hair.
- "front" or "0" = same as img1.

Mandatory constraints:
1. THE IMAGE IS ALWAYS UPRIGHT. The head is vertical in the frame — crown at the top edge, chin/neck at the bottom edge. Never sideways. Never tilted. Never rotated on the 2D plane. This is non-negotiable.
2. Framing: head and shoulders visible. Include the full top of the head (including hair) with a small margin above, down to mid-chest or collarbone area. No cropping of the top of the head, ears, chin, or hair.
3. Person centered in frame, same scale as img1.
4. Preserve identity: same face shape, facial features, skin tone, complexion, facial hair, hairstyle, hair color, hair texture, and any visible accessories (glasses, earrings, piercings, etc.). Match all colors and textures exactly.
5. Preserve visible clothing: same neckline, collar, or top as seen in img1. Match fabric, color, and pattern.
6. Same background as img1 (clean studio, solid color, or matched environment). Same soft neutral lighting. No new props, no extra shadows, no text.
7. Anatomically correct face and head from the new angle. Natural skin texture, natural ear placement, natural hairline. No artifacts, no blur, no distortion.
8. Eye-level camera, neutral portrait lens (no fisheye, no wide-angle distortion).

WARNING — common mistakes to avoid:
- DO NOT rotate or tilt the output image canvas. The photo orientation must match img1.
- DO NOT lay the head sideways in the frame.
- DO NOT zoom out to show full body. This is a headshot — head and shoulders only.
- DO NOT change the face, hairstyle, skin tone, or accessories.
- DO NOT add makeup, remove glasses, or alter any facial feature.
- DO NOT change the background style or lighting mood.
- DO NOT generate a different person. Identity preservation is critical.

a3ba0f86-9bf0-44cd-8314-075330f67e9f.text:
- Primary render prompt (hyper-realistic, runway)
  - Create a hyper-realistic high-fashion editorial image that exactly matches the provided fashion sketch: side-profile male model walking to the right, same pose, proportions, and silhouette.
  - Keep the same background as the reference: off-white/cream paper texture with faint warm watercolor blotches, subtle vignette, no added set, no extra props.
  - Outfit: a tailored, knee-length coat in soft pastel plaid (yellow base with muted pink/blue lines), structured shoulders, clean lapel-less/flat front appearance as in sketch, straight long sleeves.
  - Detail the garment construction strictly from what is visible:
    - Crisp seam lines and edge finishes where they would naturally appear (side seams, sleeve seams, hem turn-up), but do not invent extra panels.
    - Front closure: only depict closures if clearly visible; if not visible, keep the front visually clean with no buttons, no zipper, no snaps.
    - Hem: neat, slightly weighted drape; fabric reads as medium-weight wool/suiting with a soft sheen and realistic texture.
  - Orange ruffle/volume element at the left elbow area exactly as shown (textured tulle/organza-like cluster), with realistic translucency and layered edges.
  - Lower half: long coat hem revealing a pale/neutral underlayer as suggested by sketch (do not add new garments beyond what’s implied).
  - Accessories/objects: the model carries the same fish-shaped bag/object as in the sketch, with the same scale, placement, and strap/hand position; render it in realistic materials while preserving the exact shape.
  - Footwear: glossy green knee-high rubber boots (rain-boot finish), with realistic highlights, sole thickness, and shaft shape; match the sketch’s bold green tone.
  - Lighting: soft studio daylight, gentle shadow under boots, high-end editorial contrast, ultra-detailed fabric weave, clean skin texture, natural hair.
  - Camera/quality: full-body side profile, centered subject, 85mm editorial feel, ultra sharp, 8k realism, color-accurate to sketch.

- Negative prompt (do not add)
  - No new design elements: no extra pockets, belts, buttons, visible zippers, logos, embroidery, lapels, collars, epaulettes, vents, or additional seams beyond what’s implied.
  - No change to background (no runway, no street, no studio wall), no added jewelry, no hat, no sunglasses, no styling props.
  - No change to pose, direction, or silhouette; no extra garments; no pattern change beyond the pastel plaid.

- Trend-forward rendering notes (still faithful to sketch)
  - Emphasize quiet-luxury finishing: clean topstitching where appropriate, refined edge binding/turned hems, subtle fabric depth.
  - Plaid should feel woven (not printed), with realistic yarn variation and gentle warp/weft texture while keeping the sketch’s pastel palette.
  - Orange elbow volume should look couture-handled: layered, airy, with believable structure and shadowing, without enlarging or reshaping it.

modelParameters.prompt:
You analyze the attached reference image and write one final production-ready prompt for Nano Banana Pro.


The goal is to generate one single modern 6-panel drawing guide page for the exact attached image.


The attached image is the only source of truth.


The final result must preserve the exact same:
- subject
- pose
- viewing angle
- camera angle
- crop
- framing
- silhouette
- proportions
- clothing
- hair or flower shape or object shape
- facial structure or subject structure
- composition
- orientation in the frame


Do not redesign anything.
Do not beautify anything.
Do not normalize anything.
Do not improve anatomy.
Do not change the angle.
Do not change the crop.
Do not change the silhouette.
Do not change the clothing, hair, facial structure, object shape, flower structure, or body proportions.
Do not turn it into a generic portrait, generic flower, generic animal, generic object, or generic building.


The page must show exactly 6 progressive stages of drawing the exact same attached image.


All 6 panels must show the same exact subject from the same exact viewpoint, same exact crop, same exact framing, same exact proportions, and same exact silhouette.


The 6 panels are not allowed to reinterpret the image.
They are only allowed to progressively simplify and reconstruct the exact same image.


The sequence must feel beginner-friendly, logical, and easy to follow.
A person with no drawing skill should be able to understand what to do next from one panel to the next.


Each panel must introduce only one clear new level of information.
Do not let later panels repeat the same amount of detail.
Make the difference between panel 4, panel 5, and panel 6 very clear.


Use this exact construction logic:


Panel 1:
show only the biggest outer envelope and the overall placement of the subject on the page.
Use only very light guide lines.
Show the main tilt, the main bounding height and width, and the largest simple silhouette.
No details.
No features.
No small shapes.


Panel 2:
show the main structural masses inside that envelope.
Use very simple solid forms that truly match the reference image, such as oval, sphere, box, cylinder, wedge, long bean, or flat block only where appropriate.
This stage must explain the large form clearly and simply.
Do not use random abstract blobs.
Do not introduce forms that do not help a beginner understand the subject.


Panel 3:
show the essential guide system.
Add the main center line, tilt line, eye line, feature line, width checks, height checks, angle checks, and proportion guides only where they are genuinely useful for constructing this exact image.
The guides must be clean, sparse, correct, and readable.
This stage should teach measurement and alignment.


Panel 4:
show the transition from construction to recognizable form.
Connect the large masses into a believable clear structure.
Turn the primitive forms into a readable drawing scaffold.
Add secondary shapes and contour correction, but keep the drawing simple.
Do not add fine details yet.
Do not add texture yet.
This panel should answer: how do the simple forms connect into the real subject?


Panel 5:
show a simplified clean drawing with the most important features added.
Reduce the visible guide lines.
Keep only the most useful remaining construction lines.
Add the key recognizable elements that make the subject look correct, such as main facial features, main hair masses, major folds, key petal groups, or main object edges depending on the subject.
Do not fully finish the drawing.
Do not add rendering or texture.
This panel should answer: what are the essential details to make it look right?


Panel 6:
show the final clean educational sketch.
Remove almost all guide lines.
Keep the drawing clear, tidy, and hand-drawable.
Add only minimal finishing information such as slight line emphasis or very light shadow grouping if truly helpful, but do not fully render.
This panel should look like the final version a beginner could realistically aim for after following the previous five stages.


Line system must be consistent and educational across all 6 panels:
- very light lines for early placement and guides
- medium lines for major forms
- clearer but controlled lines for refined contour in later stages
- no heavy rendering
- no dark decorative shading
- no random sketch noise
- no messy overworking


Make panel progression visually distinct:
- Panel 1 = placement only
- Panel 2 = simple forms only
- Panel 3 = measuring and guides
- Panel 4 = connected structure
- Panel 5 = essential likeness
- Panel 6 = clean final sketch


All 6 panels must behave like six reductions of the same frozen frame, not six different drawings.


Each panel must keep the same subject placement and same overall bounding shape.
No panel may drift into a different version of the subject.


The visual style must be:
- modern
- minimal
- premium
- pure white background
- monochrome graphite or soft gray pencil lines
- clean consistent layout
- identical panel style across all 6 panels
- identical line style across all 6 panels
- identical spacing and composition across all 6 panels


Do not generate decorative typography.
Do not generate mixed fonts.
Do not generate handwritten notes.
Do not generate title text.
Do not generate long labels.


Best option: generate no text at all inside the page.
Only the drawings and clean panel structure.


Strictly avoid:
- vintage look
- old book look
- scanned page look
- off-white paper
- yellow paper
- print texture
- smudges
- mixed visual styles
- infographic style
- poster style
- app UI


Return only one final prompt for Nano Banana Pro.
Do not return explanations.
Do not return JSON.
Do not return notes.

19597bca-86fa-412e-9645-1aba8c4f9fe4.text: A modern minimal 6-panel progressive drawing guide on a pure white background, monochrome graphite pencil lines, clean uniform grid layout with equal spacing, showing exactly six stages of drawing the same calico cat standing on a stone ledge seen from a slightly low three-quarter front-right angle, mouth wide open hissing, tail raised high curving slightly backward, front legs extended forward in a stretched stance, hind legs slightly crouched, compact stocky body proportions, short fur, triangular ears with the left ear rotated outward, full body visible from paws to tail tip, cat facing right occupying most of the frame. Panel 1: very light barely visible guide lines only showing the overall bounding envelope of the cat silhouette, a tilted horizontal long shape for the torso, a tall upward stroke for the raised tail, four short vertical marks for leg placement, a small circle placeholder upper right for the head, no details no features just pure placement and tilt on the page. Panel 2: simple solid primitive forms replacing the envelope, an elongated oval for the ribcage-torso mass, a smaller sphere for the head tilted slightly right and down, a tapered cylinder for the raised tail curving up and back, four short cylinders for the legs with the front pair angled forward and the rear pair bent, a small wedge for the open jaw, all forms clearly separated and readable. Panel 3: clean sparse construction guides added over the forms, a center line through the torso oval showing the body tilt, a vertical center line on the head sphere, a horizontal eye line across the head, a jaw-opening angle line, proportion tick marks showing head-to-body ratio, shoulder and hip width markers, tail curvature arc guide, leg length comparison lines, all drawn in very light thin lines. Panel 4: primitive forms connected into a believable cat silhouette, smooth contour linking head to neck to shoulders to back to raised tail, chest and belly curve connected, front leg contour shaped with paw angles, rear legs shaped with hock bend, ear triangles placed, open mouth shape refined into upper and lower jaw, secondary masses for the haunches and chest fluff indicated, still no fine detail or texture. Panel 5: simplified clean drawing with key recognizable features added, green eyes indicated with small almond shapes, nose and open mouth with visible teeth and tongue drawn clearly, inner ear shapes, individual toes on paws, tail fur volume, the distinctive calico patch boundaries lightly mapped as contour zones on the back and tail, whiskers suggested, most construction lines reduced to faint traces, confident medium-weight contour lines. Panel 6: final clean educational sketch with nearly all guide lines removed, refined confident outlines, slight line weight variation emphasizing the jaw opening and tail curve and leg stance, very light minimal shadow grouping under the belly and between the legs and under the chin, patch zones on back and tail indicated with the lightest pencil tone, clean tidy hand-drawable result a beginner could realistically achieve. No text no labels no titles no typography no decorative elements, identical panel size and spacing, consistent line style across all six panels, no vintage texture no yellow paper no smudges no rendering no heavy shading.
